node.title: How can I learn difficult material so it lasts?
node.content: Lasting learning means you can retrieve an idea later, explain why it works, and use it in a different situation—not merely recognize it while notes are open.

node.title: The real goal: usable knowledge
node.content:
Test learning at three levels:

  • Recall: reconstruct it without cues
  • Explanation: make the causal steps clear
  • Transfer: use it on an unfamiliar case

Familiarity can imitate mastery while material is visible.

node.title: Retrieval builds later access
node.content:
Trying to reconstruct an answer is itself a learning event. Classroom evidence finds a moderate average benefit from quizzing, but the effect depends on feedback, repetition, task format, and successful initial retrieval.

Rule: attempt first; reveal second.

node.title: Spacing makes retrieval durable
node.content: Revisit after some forgetting so the idea must be reconstructed rather than echoed from short-term context. There is no universal best interval: useful gaps grow with the desired retention horizon and shrink after failure.

node.title: Retrieve, check, and repair
node.content: Commit to an answer before checking it. Then record the error, why it happened, and the corrected reasoning. Feedback matters most when retrieval is difficult or plausible wrong answers could become familiar.

node.title: Protect sleep; skip the hacks
node.content:
Restricted sleep modestly impairs memory formation, and sleep supports consolidation through several interacting mechanisms. Effects vary by task, age, timing, and encoding strength.

Defensible advice: protect adequate sleep before and after demanding learning—not rigid REM, deep-sleep, or audio-cue recipes.

node.title: The LASTS protocol
node.content:
• L — Locate a performance target
  • A — Attempt before review
  • S — Study only the gaps
  • T — Test from memory over time
  • S — Switch contexts and problem types

Learning lasts when you repeatedly reconstruct, correct, and use an idea under changing conditions.

node.title: Where the simple story breaks
node.content:
• Retrieval can strengthen answers without producing far transfer.
  • It cannot replace initial comprehension or worked examples.
  • Uncorrected testing can stabilize errors.
  • Harder is not always better for novices or anxious learners.
  • Sleep supports memory but does not guarantee it.

node.title: A 35-minute learning session
node.content:
• 3 min: define what you must do unaided
  • 7 min: make a cold attempt
  • 10 min: study only missing links
  • 10 min: retrieve closed-book
  • 5 min: log errors and schedule the next test

node.title: A spacing schedule you can keep
node.content:
Try retrieval after roughly 1 → 3 → 7 → 14 → 30 days. Increase the gap after fluent success; shorten it or add cues after failure.

Choose intervals from the date you need the knowledge—not from a universal percentage rule.

node.title: Make knowledge transferable
node.content:
Change the cue, example, and problem format. Compare near-neighbors, explain causal steps, and solve one unfamiliar case without help.

Transfer is more likely when retrieval itself requires elaboration; it weakens as the new task becomes less like the practiced one.

node.title: The mastery check
node.content:
Without notes, can you:

  • explain it simply;
  • reconstruct the key steps;
  • solve a novel case;
  • state where it stops applying;
  • calibrate your confidence?

A miss is useful data: feed that gap into the next cycle.

node.title: Testing boosts classroom learning
node.content:
Across 48,478 students and 222 independent studies, quizzing improved achievement by a medium amount versus controls (Hedges’ g ≈ 0.50), with meaningful moderator effects.

Yang et al., 2021

node.title: Testing beats restudy after a delay
node.content:
Rereading looked better after five minutes, while retrieval practice produced better recall after two days and one week—and rereading inflated confidence.

Roediger & Karpicke, 2006

node.title: Spacing depends on the retention horizon
node.content:
A synthesis of 839 assessments found that the spacing gap and desired retention interval jointly determine later recall. A recent classroom meta-analysis found a moderate average benefit but very high heterogeneity.

Cepeda et al., 2006 · Mawson & Kang, 2025

node.title: Retrieval transfer has boundaries
node.content:
Transfer is positive on average but strongly moderated by response match, elaboration, and initial performance. Effects weaken for unpracticed material and more distant applications.

Pan & Rickard, 2018

node.title: Sleep supports memory—with variation
node.content:
A 2024 meta-analysis found a small impairment to memory formation from sleep restriction. A 2025 synthesis describes active consolidation alongside reduced interference and synaptic reorganization.

Crowley et al., 2024 · Lutz, Harkotte & Born, 2025
